# The Gate at the Door

Everything in the earlier books was, in a sense, an argument about what ought
to be true. Names ought to conform. Authority ought to follow the
organizational coordinate. Markings that do not belong in canon ought never
to land in it. Scripts that govern the estate ought to be signed. Arguments
about what *ought* to be true are the substance of governance, but they are
also its weakness, because an argument cannot stop a commit. A gate can. The
server-side hook is where the entire series stops being a position paper and
becomes a thing that either accepts your change or refuses it.

At the moment a push arrives, before a single object becomes canon, the host
runs the rules. A change to a protected branch is permitted only to those who
hold stewardship over canon; everyone else may propose, but not decide. A
new canonical document must carry frontmatter that validates against the
schema, or it does not land. A filename must match the convention the corpus
depends on, or it is rejected at the door. Markings that have no place in the
governance record are refused outright. A script that would govern the estate
but carries no trusted signature is turned away. None of this is advisory.
It is the difference between a policy that lives in a document and a policy
that lives in the path a commit must walk to exist.

This is the inversion the series has been circling from the first book. For
decades the organizational structure lived in people's heads and in the tribal
knowledge of whoever had been there longest, enforced — when it was enforced
at all — by review, by habit, by the hope that everyone remembered the rule.
Here the rule is the gate. The coordinate is not a label that a careful
operator remembers to apply; it is a condition the commit must satisfy to
become real. Governance stops being a practice that depends on diligence and
becomes a property of the substrate itself.

And the authority behind the gate is not maintained by hand. The teams that
decide who may steward, who may write, and who may only read are not lists an
administrator curates and forgets to prune. They are the organizational
coordinate, arriving as it always does: a group claim from the modern tenant
becomes team membership on the host, and a mover event in the HR feed
propagates to repository permission within minutes, without anyone touching
the Git service at all. When someone changes roles, their power over canon
changes with them, automatically, because the path computes it. The series
called this the dream of a single organizational truth expressed everywhere;
at the gate, it is simply how the door decides whom to open for.

The host now holds canon, faces the network through one watched door, runs
under an identity the directory issues, and enforces the governance corpus at
the instant of the commit. What remains is to say plainly that this is real —
and to point to where it is built.
